extracted.intended_audience: public relations managers, practitioners, and students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying publics, setting objectives, budgeting (time and money), and selecting/monitoring public relations program alternatives using Grunig's situational theory and management techniques (PPBS, zero-based budgeting, Gantt, PERT, CPM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication 1: Avoid programs for low-probability publics
rubrics_metrics.description: When a public has a low probability of information seeking and processing and a low probability that messages directed at it will be effective, seldom should you spend time and money on a public relations program to reach that public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No one will be listening or acting; prioritize resources away from such publics unless other considerations intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication 2: Address low-probability but high-consequence publics selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: If a low-probability public is important because it can have a severe consequence for the organization (e.g., linked by an enabling linkage), you may reach it through information processing but should not expect active information seeking or full message effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect only partial message retention; even partial retention may stimulate problem recognition and move members toward seeking/processing; design messages accordingly and monitor for emergence of awareness or activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication 3: Tailor communication strategy to processing vs seeking publics
rubrics_metrics.description: For publics that will process rather than seek information, you need a different strategy: active communicators look for and try to understand information; passive publics do not look for information and will do little to understand randomly delivered information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use style and creativity (photos, illustrations, clever writing, catchy phrases, slogans) to lure passive publics into processing; rely on substance and accessibility for those who actively seek information (example: Sam Adams historically used attention-getting tactics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication 4: Actively communicate with active publics
rubrics_metrics.description: With active publics (high probability of information seeking and behavior), the organization cannot maintain a low public profile; if you do not communicate, these publics will seek information elsewhere and form cognitions/attitudes/behaviors from other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively provide your organization's point of view because other sources may present the organization poorly; sustaining communication is essential with active publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication 5: Focus attitude/behavior-change objectives on high-probability publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not expect cognition, attitude, and behavior changes from many members of your publics; only aware and active publics (e.g., high-involvement, problem-facing) typically develop reasoned cognitions/attitudes and engage in behavior — at most about 40% go that far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your objective is attitude or behavior change (e.g., fundraising), concentrate on publics with the highest probability of attitude/behavior formation; active publics are difficult to persuade and may adopt negative as well as positive positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public typology: Active on all issues (activist publics)
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of people who are high-involvement and problem-facing across multiple issues (e.g., activists who challenge organizations on many issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat them as consistently engaged stakeholders; expect sustained scrutiny and cross-issue attention; plan broad, consistent communication strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public typology: Apathetic on all issues (nonpublics)
rubrics_metrics.description: People who are nonpublics — low-involvement and fatalistic behavior — across all issues to which the theory is applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations generally need pay no attention to these publics for the given issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public typology: Active only on widely-shared issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Publics that are apathetic about most issues but become active when an issue affects nearly everyone in the population (e.g., gasoline shortage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These publics may require temporary, issue-specific communications; consider broad-reach tactics when such universally relevant issues arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public typology: Single-issue publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Publics that crusade for one issue doggedly while ignoring other issues (e.g., infant-formula controversy, whale-killing controversy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat them as focused stakeholders with sustained attention on one topic; anticipate persistent pressure and design targeted responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine baseline knowledge, attitudes, behaviors (formative research)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the time research identifies publics, managers should ask members how much they know about the organization, what ideas and attitudes they hold, and what behaviors they practice to determine how much communication objectives have already been met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formative research to decide whether to supply new information, correct misinformation, or to change vs reinforce existing attitudes/behaviors; results inform objective-setting and program design (see evaluation research for measuring objectives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the behavioral molecule stages in program planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan public relations programs through the behavioral molecule stages: detect a public relations problem, construct (define the problem, formulate objectives, develop alternative solutions), select (choose alternatives), confirm (approve and allocate resources), and behave (implement and monitor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budgets and time estimates should be prepared in the define segment, selected in the select segment, confirmed for authority in confirm, and used for monitoring in behave; avoid skipping stages (e.g., implementing without proper define/select/confirm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative vs program budgets
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the administrative budget (budget for the entire public relations department; usually annual) from program budgets (budgets for specific PR programs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heads of PR must develop administrative budgets built from program budgets prepared by middle managers; show how department programs support organizational goals when seeking approval from higher management or a budget committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: PPBS (Planning-Programming-Budgeting System)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bottom-up budgeting system: planning (define goals and methods), programming (schedule and implement projects), budgeting (attach price estimates to goals, plans, programs, projects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop programs to meet objectives and prepare program budgets that then aggregate into the departmental administrative budget; contrasts with top-down approaches where allocations constrain program choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero-based budgeting
rubrics_metrics.description: A PPBS variation requiring managers to start budgets and program justifications 'from zero' as if no prior budgets/programs exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forces reexamination of whether existing programs are still needed and alignment with current organizational goals and PR problems; use periodically (e.g., every 3–5 years) rather than annually to avoid undue disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget category: Salaries and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate the proportion of full-time employees' time (and associated salary/benefits) spent on each program; include part-time employees and consultants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine time allocation accurately and charge program accordingly; personnel costs often constitute a major portion of program budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget category: Production
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs for printing, typesetting, art/design, photographs, audiovisual materials, purchase of media time/space, reproduction of press releases, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate production needs early; different program types (employee, community, educational relations) will have different production profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget category: Equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs of new equipment required for a program or maintenance/depreciation of existing equipment used by the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include capital and recurring equipment-related costs; account for depreciation or leasing where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget category: Overhead
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate a percentage of rent, postage, telephone, utilities, etc., to each program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a consistent method to apportion overhead across programs so program costs reflect real resource use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget category: Special project costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs unique to particular programs (e.g., renting a hotel room for a press conference, exhibit space, meals/snacks at open houses, membership fees, contributions to community programs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify program-specific expenses early and include them explicitly rather than burying them in miscellaneous lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget category: Travel
rubrics_metrics.description: Local and out-of-town travel costs necessary for each program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate travel needs and include per diem, transportation, lodging, and incidental expenses where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget category: Other costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Unique expenses not covered by other categories; determine and include them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom-tailor this line item to the specific program; avoid leaving significant items uncategorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use budget in confirm and behave segments (approval and monitoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Final budget approval (confirm) gives authority to proceed; in the behave segment use the approved budget to monitor progress and spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously check for budget overruns; if expenditures exceed budgeted amounts, stop the program and reevaluate whether it can meet objectives within the budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network analysis technique: Gantt charts
rubrics_metrics.description: A chart showing activities on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis; activities are sequenced top-to-bottom; horizontal lines show planned duration (and optionally an actual-duration line underneath).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Gantt charts for simple projects and to track actual vs planned time; useful for keeping a running record of progress and identifying schedule slippage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network analysis technique: PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses a network diagram of events (circles — start/completion markers that do not consume resources) and activities (arrows — tasks that consume time/personnel/resources); commonly used for planning large or novel projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the diagram (often working backward), estimate time for each activity (hours/days/months), and (typically) make three time estimates per activity: optimistic (O), most likely (M), pessimistic (P). Compute the expected time Te using Te = (O + 4M + P) / 6 (a weighted average). PERT yields a 50% probable completion estimate; compute variance and use statistical tables for other confidence levels if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the critical path and manage slack
rubrics_metrics.description: After estimating activity times, sum times along each path; the longest path is the critical path and determines the shortest possible project completion time. Noncritical paths have slack (excess time) that provides scheduling flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus management attention and resources on activities on the critical path because delays there lengthen the project. Use slack on noncritical paths to reallocate resources temporarily; be aware that shortening one path may expose a different critical path.

rubrics_metrics.name: CPM (Critical Path Method) and crashing
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar to PERT but focused on minimizing project time and cost of shortening it: estimate normal time and crash time for activities; construct crash-time network to find minimum possible project time, then iteratively 'crash' activities on the critical path with the lowest crash cost until you reach the shortest feasible project time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate crash costs for activities; choose the least-cost crash options on the current critical path and re-evaluate the critical path after each change to find the minimum crash cost for the desired project duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-making: select alternatives by comparing costs, benefits, and time
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying publics, defining alternative programs, and budgeting money and time for each alternative, select which alternative(s) to implement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the define/select/confirm stages to compare program effectiveness, efficiency, time-to-complete, and alignment with objectives; select alternatives that maximize desired outcomes within resource/time constraints.
